current.rappels: Not recommended to rappel directly (angled rappels off single bolts, rope-length issues); standard descent rappels Mile High Club instead with a single 60m rope.
current.rappel_count_note: Eight rappels down Mile High Club's line on a single 60 m rope. That configuration is newer than the route: a dedicated rappel line was added alongside Mile High Club in August 2019 specifically so the descent could be done on a single 60, and the eight-station descent dates from then. Before that, parties used a single 70 m or two 60 m ropes, and counts from that era differ honestly - eight single-rope rappels on a 70, or seven - so an older count disagreeing with this table describes the pre-2019 descent, not an error. The line stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line throughout, and you should prefer the skier's-left anchor wherever two exist, because most stations are doubled so that rappelling and climbing parties are not on the same anchor. Beyond Redlining is equipped for rappelling but its own line is explicitly not recommended: the first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it requires angling rappels off single bolts where many rappels only reach the next anchor on rope stretch. Beyond Redlining's own hardware - a mid-pitch-1 bail station, a missing maillon on pitch 3 - belongs to that line and not to this one. No per-station rappel distances are known for the Mile High Club descent, and the rappel line does not follow the climbing line, so the pitch lengths are not a substitute; the figures given are nominal rather than measured.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope end has jammed in a crack on the right side of this rappel, forcing the party to climb back up the other strand to free it - and the ground you would climb to reach it is loose. Watch where the ends land and pull away from the crack.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the shared summit down to the P7 anchor on Mile High Club's line; single 60m rope reaches comfortably.
rappel_detail.anchor: summit rap rings, station ~8ft south of summit bolts and ~4ft off the ground
hazards: The edge below this station has cut a rope badly enough that the party had to chop it in half and retire it. The route page says the edge has since been ground down; the Beyond Redlining page still tells you exactly where to lay the rope, so treat it as live

A hard pendulum. The first-ascent advice is to lower to the large flake and walk left to the belay rather than rappelling free; a 2025 party swung hard right into a separate rock face on this rappel, on both of their visits
The nuts on these rap rings have been found loose - check them before you weight the station

Rappelling Beyond Redlining's own line is what this station exists to avoid: its first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it needs angling rappels off single bolts, many of which only reach the next anchor on rope stretch
rappel_detail.station: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings sit back from the route's top, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down toward the lower anchor sitting at the foot of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.

rappel_detail.notes: A face-descent rappel down to the P6 anchor.
hazards: Dropping to the dihedral-top anchor instead is a specific, named mistake - the station you want is above and left of it
The published reason for tossing left is that parties climb directly below: keep the rope and anything you knock loose off them
rappel_detail.station: Toss the rope slightly left of the bolt line rather than straight down. Rappel the pitch-6 face, then move to a rap anchor about 10 ft skier's left and 10 ft higher than the anchor atop the dihedral pitch. Do not continue to the top of the dihedral pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: A short rappel down to a ledge at P5; source explicitly flags this one as short.
hazards: Free-hanging above a ledge, so you arrive spinning onto a stance rather than sliding onto it
rappel_detail.station: A short rappel from the pitch-5 station to an anchor on a ledge off to the side of the dihedral pitch. It is free-hanging above the ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to P4, where one of two available anchor options is used.
hazards: Most stations on this route have two anchors a few feet apart so ascending and descending parties do not share one - taking the wrong one puts you on top of climbers
Rope thrown from here lands on anyone on pitch 4 below
rappel_detail.station: Two anchors are available here; take the skier's-left one where you can, which keeps you off the climbing line.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope has been stuck in a crack pulling from the pitch-3 rap anchors; pull away from the crack. Feed the rope through the cedar bushes rather than throwing it.
rappel_detail.notes: The most commonly botched rappel on the descent — aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line; a hidden intermediate anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the visible upper-P3 station.
hazards: The route page states it outright: do not rappel down the vertical face on a single rope, because you will not reach the next anchors. Parties who miss it end up either doing two double-rope rappels from the top of pitch 3 or, on an 80 m, nearly reaching the pitch-2 anchors and then having to scramble across exposed ground
One party that missed it could not retrieve their rope at all - the pull angle around the intervening features made it stick and recovering it was judged unsafe
The tree the beta says will be flagged has never been flagged; years later the beta still only promises that it will be flagged soon
rappel_detail.station: The confusing one, and by a wide margin the most-reported problem on this descent. From the pitch-4 anchor, pass through cedar bushes directly below the station and rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3 - it is mostly walking. Aim for a tree about 10 ft tall standing roughly 15 ft skier's left of the climbing line; the intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree. Look for it right where the ground turns from slabby to vertical. You cannot see this anchor on the way up, so it cannot be scouted on the climb; parties have found chalk arrows pointing at it.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down to a lower-P3 anchor, landing on a large ledge.
hazards: This is the vertical face the station above exists to get you onto safely; it is the ground you would be stranded above having missed the nook
rappel_detail.station: From the nook anchor, rappel the vertical section at the start of pitch 3 down to a large ledge, and set up at one of the anchors on top of pitch 2 - the skier's-left one if it is free.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to the P2 anchor.
hazards: Parties consistently record being surprised that the last anchor before the ground is a separate one, offset from the climbing anchor
rappel_detail.station: The station is NOT the pitch-1 climbing anchor, which is what people expect and head for. The rap anchor is about 10 ft down and 10-15 ft skier's left of the pitch-1 belay anchor.

rappel_detail.pull: Consider staying on rappel, walking back across to the belay bolt where the route starts, and pulling the rope from there.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel(s) via the P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base of the route.
hazards: Do not treat the base of the route as the ground - the ledge you land on is exposed and hundreds of feet up
The gully to climber's right throws natural rockfall onto the start of the scramble; keep helmets on until you are clear of it, especially with parties above
rappel_detail.station: The last rappel reaches the base of the route. Expect the starting ledge to be quite exposed, several hundred feet off the ground.

current.descent_text: Do not rappel Beyond Redlining itself — official route beta explicitly says it is equipped for emergency use but 'not recommended' as a descent line, since the angle and pitch lengths make it a poor rap line that would need two ropes or a 70m rope with awkward hangs. Instead, from the shared summit, descend via Mile High Club's dedicated rappel line, which works with a single 60m rope over 8 rappels: summit rap rings down through P7, P6 (face descent), a short rap on P5 to a ledge, P4 to one of two available anchors, then the tricky 'upper P3' rappel — this one is the most commonly botched: aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line, where a hidden intermediate P3 anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the station; missing it and rapping straight down the vertical face below can leave you well short of the next anchor on a single rope. Below that, a lower-P3 rap drops to a large ledge, then P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base. The first rap station off the summit is set back roughly 8 ft south of the summit bolts and about 4 ft off the ground — easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. Saddlebag your rope on the way down to avoid dropping loose rock or gear on parties below; ledges on this face hold loose material. Because Beyond Redlining offers limited bail options low on the route, parties should carry a 70m rope if there's any real chance of needing to retreat mid-climb rather than topping out to the shared summit.

current.rappels: 8 single-rope rappels with a 60m (or 70m) rope; a critical intermediate anchor partway up P3 must not be missed on descent.
current.rappel_count_note: Eight single-strand rappels off fixed bolted anchors, and a single 60 m rope is documented as sufficient for every one of them (a 70 m gives more margin). Two 60 m ropes also work and are the recommended insurance for one specific reason: if you miss the intermediate anchor in the nook below the small tree on rap 5 and continue down the vertical face, a single-rope party cannot reach the next anchors. The rap line is not the climbing line — it stays roughly 3-5 m skier's left of the bolts for the whole descent, so anchors are found left of where you climbed and pulls are never plumb.

rappel_detail.pull: Nothing on this descent pulls plumb, because the anchors zigzag left of the bolts. Flick the strands clear of the bolt line before pulling or they hang up on hardware.
rappel_detail.notes: Drops to the anchor at the base of pitch 7.
hazards: There is an edge right at the start. It has since been ground down, but put the rope over the least sharp part of it anyway.
Loose rock sits on several of the belay ledges on this route; stack ropes so you are not sweeping it off onto the party below.
rappel_detail.station: Rap rings set back from the summit at the top of pitch 7. The rappel runs diagonally down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7, which is the pattern for the whole descent: the rap line sits roughly 3-5 m (10-15 ft) skier's left of the bolted climbing line the entire way down.

rappel_detail.notes: Face rappel.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted anchor left and above the dihedral
hazards: Throw the rope slightly left of the bolt line: climbers coming up are directly beneath, and rope thrown down the line takes loose rock with it.
rappel_detail.station: Rappel down the face to an anchor set about 3 m left of and 3 m above the top of the dihedral. Do not stop at the top of the dihedral itself — the anchor you want is above and left of it.

rappel_detail.notes: Short drop to a ledge.
rappel_detail.anchor: Ledge-side bolted anchor beside the dihedral
hazards: Free-hanging finish onto a ledge — control the swing rather than arriving sideways.
Loose rock on the ledge.
rappel_detail.station: A short rappel to the anchor on the ledge beside the dihedral pitch. The last part of it hangs free above the ledge, so expect a spin before your feet find anything.

rappel_detail.notes: Two anchor options exist at this stance.
rappel_detail.anchor: One of two bolted anchors at the pitch 4 stance
hazards: Choosing the right-hand anchor drops your ropes onto anyone climbing, which is why the left is the published preference.
rappel_detail.station: Two anchors exist at the pitch 4 stance. Take the skier's-left one; the right-hand option puts your ropes across the climbing line.

rappel_detail.pull: Two ropes make the consequence of missing the nook recoverable; on a single rope it is not.
rappel_detail.notes: Short, free-hanging rappel aimed at a ~10ft tree left of the line.
hazards: Missing this station and continuing down the vertical face below it leaves a party on a single rope unable to reach the next anchors. This is the one place on the descent where a route-finding error strands you mid-face, and the route description flags it explicitly.
The cedar bushes hide both the anchor and the rope; do not rappel past on autopilot because the terrain is low-angle here.
rappel_detail.station: The station people miss, and the one that matters most. Push through the cedar bushes directly below the anchor above, rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3, and aim for a tree about 3 m tall standing roughly 5 m skier's left of the climbing line. The intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree.

rappel_detail.notes: Vertical face rappel down lower pitch 3.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted anchor at a large ledge, pitch 2 anchors
hazards: This is the steep face the previous warning is about — you are now committed below the nook.
Loose rock on the large ledge.
rappel_detail.station: From the nook anchor, down the vertical face of lower pitch 3 to the large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors. Take the left anchor if it is free.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to the pitch 1 station.
hazards: Easy to arrive at the belay rather than the rap station and burn time traversing across on a slabby stance.
rappel_detail.station: Drops to the pitch 1 rappel anchor, which is about 3 m below and 3-5 m skier's left of the pitch 1 belay bolts — not the belay itself.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel to the ground; a single 70m rope is sufficient for the whole sequence.
hazards: The base ledge is exposed above a long drop. Stay roped, walk back to the belay bolt and pull the rope from there rather than coming off the system on the ledge.
Keep helmets on: on a route this popular there is usually still a party above you when you land.
In spring the approach gully below still holds steep snow, which complicates the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.
rappel_detail.station: Last rappel to the start of the route. The starting ledge is several hundred feet above the ground and genuinely exposed, so this is not a place to untie casually.

current.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the route itself, back down the same line you climbed — do not try to walk off. Eight single-strand rappels, all off bolted, fixed anchors (this is a sport-bolted line, so no natural gear or v-threads needed): rap 1 from the P7/summit anchor down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7; rap 2 face-rappels to an anchor set left and above the dihedral; rap 3 is a short drop to a ledge-side anchor beside the dihedral; rap 4 goes to one of two anchors at the pitch 4 stance (favor the left one); rap 5 is a short, free-hanging rap off an upper-P3 anchor aimed at a ~10 ft tree left of the line, with an intermediate anchor in a nook below it; rap 6 is a vertical face rappel down lower P3 to a large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors; rap 7 drops to the pitch 1 anchor (10–15 ft left of the original belay); rap 8 finishes at the base. A single 70m rope is sufficient for all 8 raps; two 60m ropes also work if you'd rather split gear or prefer doubled-rope security, and some parties carry a single 60m instead but report tighter/more numerous transitions. Because you rappel the entire route back to the start, many parties leave approach shoes and packs stashed at the base. Descent hazards: loose rock sitting on several of the belay ledges (manage ropes and stack carefully to avoid kicking debris onto the party below), some rope-stretch/rope-snag potential given the zigzagging (not straight-down) line of anchors, and lingering steep snow in the approach gully in spring that can complicate the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.

current.rappels: Most parties make three rappels on a single 60 m rope used doubled: about 25 m from the newer bolted anchor on the ridge crest down to the platform, then two of about 30 m down the Class 4 gully past the chockstone to its base. Some parties rappel twice and downclimb the lower gully instead. A second rope makes linking the stations easier but is not required.

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel from the bolted ridge-crest anchor down to a large ledge/platform.
Second rappel continuing down the Class 4 gully.
Third rappel reaching the base of the route; a single 60m rope used doubled covers all three rappel distances.

current.descent_text: Reverse the exposed Class 3 ridge-crest scramble/downclimb back to the top of the technical ground, then begin rappelling. The first rappel drops from a bolted anchor on the ridge crest - parties describe a solid, relatively new 2-bolt station, but also note nearby older rusted 1/4-inch bolts and pitons that should NOT be trusted, so identify the anchor carefully before weighting it - down about 25 meters to a large ledge/platform. From the platform, two more rappels of roughly 30 meters each continue down the Class 4 gully (past the chockstone/tunnel squeeze used on the way up) to reach the base of the route, for three rappels total. A single 60m rope, used doubled, comfortably covers all three rappel distances; a 50m rope has been used but is tight on the longer stretches and some parties add a short bit of roped downclimbing near the top to make it work - bring 60m if you have the choice. From the base of the climb, reverse the connecting gully and the Class 4 step back over Beta Peak's notch to Needle Pass (no further rappelling needed here, just careful downclimbing/scrambling), then downclimb or plunge-step the snow couloir back down to Gladys Divide - soft afternoon snow sometimes allows a short glissade, but the icy, rocky runout makes this a judgment call rather than a given - and walk out via Flapjack Lakes to Staircase.

current.rappels: At least a dozen rappels documented on the first ascent, mostly double-rope raps off the lower towers and gendarmes. No fixed anchors — natural gear and tat only.
current.rappel_count_note: Roughly a dozen rappels (12-13) are described getting off gendarmes/pinnacles along Mongo Ridge; a rap rope has been reported severed by rockfall on a marginal anchor somewhere along this stretch, so treat every anchor with suspicion. Individual rappel lengths are not known, so no per-station length is shown.

rappel_detail.pull: Short — the least demanding of the tower rappels, and the one that sets expectations too low for the three above it.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off a major gendarme on the ridge crest, on the way up the buttress.
rappel_detail.station: Off the first tower on the ridge.

rappel_detail.pull: About 40 m, so a single 60 m doubled does not reach. Parties either carry a second line, or rappel as far as one rope allows and then build a second station or belay the last stretch of low fifth class down to the notch.
rappel_detail.notes: Continues past another pinnacle; anchors are improvised rather than fixed stations.
rappel_detail.station: Off the second tower into the notch below it.

rappel_detail.pull: About 40 m again — same problem and same two workarounds if you are on a single rope.
rappel_detail.notes: Rockfall risk noted along this ridge; back up marginal-looking anchors where possible.
rappel_detail.station: Off the third tower.

rappel_detail.pull: Closer to 50 m, the longest of the tower rappels. On one rope this is the one most likely to leave you hanging above the notch.
rappel_detail.notes: Getting off this notch/gendarme is effectively irreversible once ropes are pulled.
rappel_detail.station: Off the fourth tower.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 5 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.
rappel_detail.station: Off tower 5 along the crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 6 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.
rappel_detail.station: Off tower 6 along the crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 7 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.
rappel_detail.station: Off tower 7 along the crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 8 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.
rappel_detail.station: Off tower 8 along the crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 9 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.
rappel_detail.station: Off tower 9 along the crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 10 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.
rappel_detail.station: Off tower 10 along the crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 11 of about 12, off another tower or gendarme on the crest into the notch below it. No individual description of this rappel is published; build the anchor from what the tower offers and expect loose rock.
rappel_detail.station: Off tower 11 along the crest.

rappel_detail.pull: Carry a good length of cord. The single-strand anchors left here have been found in poor shape a year later, and have since been rebuilt redundant — assume you will be replacing rather than clipping.
rappel_detail.notes: Off the Pole of Remoteness, the last major tower before the false summit; easier ground then leads toward West Fury's summit.
hazards: Rockfall on this rappel severed a rope on the first ascent. Having a second line in the system is what made that survivable
rappel_detail.station: Off the top of the Pole of Remoteness. The anchor is a large block on the summit of the tower; parties have tested it deliberately before committing to it.

current.descent_text: From the West Fury summit, reverse across the long, gendarme-studded connecting ridge back to East Fury, then descend East Fury via the Southeast Glacier route toward Luna Pass/Access Creek (downclimb/running-belay the summit snow, retrace the glacier, regain the Northeast Ridge, and reverse the heather-chute/rocky-rib traverse back to Luna Pass). The technical crux of the descent is the connecting ridge back to East Fury: it crosses three loose towers, climbing over each and rappelling down its far side. The dozen-odd rappels off Mongo Ridge's own gendarmes, including the Pole of Remoteness, come during the ascent, not on the way down. Anchors are almost entirely improvised: loose blocks, horns, and existing tat/slings left by prior parties rather than bolted or fixed stations, so bring a rack of slings/cord and expect to build or reinforce anchors yourself. Rockfall and rope damage on marginal block anchors have been reported (a rappel rope was severed by rockfall on the first ascent), so treat every anchor with suspicion and back it up where the rock quality is poor. Because each rappel is essentially irreversible once ropes are pulled, retreat gets progressively harder the farther a party commits along the ridge — this is a significant objective hazard if weather deteriorates. Once back at Luna Pass, retrace the approach: heather/talus traverse and scree descent to Access Col, the steep 1,800-ft descent into Access Basin, the Access Creek bushwhack back down to Big Beaver Creek, and the 11.5-mile Big Beaver Creek Trail out to the Ross Lake water taxi and Ross Dam Trailhead.

current.rappels: 2-5 rappels through the Kautz ice chute, depending on conditions and how much rope you carry: 1-3 down the upper ice step and 1-2 down the lower one, all on V-thread anchors you thread yourself. The four stations listed here are a representative middle count for a party on a single 60 m rope - fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching.
current.rappel_count_note: The count ranges from 2-5 rappels total, depending on rope length/number of ropes carried: 1-3 on the upper ice step, 1-2 on the lower ice step. 4 is used here as a representative middle count for a party on a single 60m rope; fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching.

rappel_detail.notes: First of 1-3 rappels down the upper ice step (up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice); V-thread anchors leave no gear behind and are not left in place between ascent and descent.
Continue down the upper ice step; belay to easier ground climber's-left/east into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice.
First of 1-2 rappels down the lower ice step, same anchor style as above.
Final rappel through the lower ice step; after the chute, move fast across the traverse back toward the Rock Step since this stretch sits under the active Kautz Ice Cliff.

current.descent_text: Descending the Kautz is a real technical descent, not a walk-off, and involves multiple rappels through the ice chute — typically two to five depending on conditions, ice quality, and rope length. From the top of Wapowety Cleaver, parties reverse the glacier line down through crevassed terrain to the top of the ice chute, then find easier ground to climber's-left/east to belay into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice. The upper ice step (commonly a short pitch up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice) is rappelled: the NPS route brief states this takes anywhere from one to three rappels depending on rope length and how many ropes the team carries, using 'Zero-Thread' ice anchors — a variant of the V-thread/Abalakov anchor chosen because it's equally strong but leaves no gear behind; there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route, and the Park Service explicitly discourages leaving V-thread anchors in place between ascent and descent since they can melt out. Below the upper step, lower-angle snow leads to the lower ice step, typically descended with one to two more rappels on the same anchor style — so two to five rappels total through the chute is realistic for most parties on a single 60m rope, fewer with two ropes or more if short-pitching. After the chute, a fast, alert traverse back toward the Rock Step is required, since this stretch sits directly under the active Kautz Ice Cliff. Climbing back up through the Rock Step itself (awkward 5th-class moves protected by fixed rope and old slings on rock anchors) returns parties to high camp; from there it's a walk/glissade down the Turtle Snowfield, back across the Nisqually or Wilson glacier crossing, and out to Paradise (or back down through Van Trump Park). A significant number of teams instead choose the 'up-and-over' option — descending the easier, non-technical Disappointment Cleaver/Muir Snowfield line from the summit to Camp Muir and Paradise — specifically to avoid re-descending the ice chute and Rock Step on tired legs, at the cost of having to haul full camping gear over the summit.

current.rappels: 2-5 rappels through the Kautz ice steps on the way down, depending on conditions and how much rope you carry: 1-3 down the upper ice step and 1-2 down the lower one, all on ice anchors you build yourself. The four stations listed are a middle count for a party on a single 60 m rope; with two 60 m ropes it can be as few as two, plus some downclimbing.
current.rappel_count_note: The count ranges from 2-5 rappels total, depending on rope length/number of ropes carried: 1-3 on the upper ice step, 1-2 on the lower ice step. 4 is used here as a representative middle count for a party on a single 60m rope; fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching. With two 60 m ropes, two double-rope rappels plus some downclimbing get most parties through the steepest ice.

rappel_detail.notes: First of 1-3 rappels down the upper ice step (up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice); V-thread anchors leave no gear behind and are not left in place between ascent and descent.
Continue down the upper ice step; belay to easier ground climber's-left/east into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice.
First of 1-2 rappels down the lower ice step, same anchor style as above.
Final rappel through the lower ice step; after the chute, move fast across the traverse back toward the Rock Step since this stretch sits under the active Kautz Ice Cliff.

current.descent_text: Descent is normally either back down the Kautz Glacier itself (the way you came) or a carryover down the Disappointment Cleaver route to Paradise. On the headwall's ice steps specifically, with 60m ropes two double-rope rappels plus some downclimbing are enough to get back down through the steepest sections to the base of the ice pitches — rappel anchors on the ice steps are typically ice (V-thread/zero-thread) anchors, the modern standard, not fixed bolts — old ascent-placed threads should not be reused. Expect 1-3 rappels through the upper step and 1-2 more through the lower step. This is a snow/ice route with no permanent hardware. In marginal conditions, some parties place running belays or fix a line through the ice steps instead of full rappels, both for the descent and to assist less-experienced members. Below the headwall, the Kautz/Wilson Glacier descent back to the Turtle or out via Comet Falls involves standard roped glacier travel, not further rappelling.

current.rappels: Numerous short, traverse-y rappels down the south ridge (or downclimb/simul-downclimb); clip existing rap stations and back up old webbing as needed
current.rappel_count_note: Reported as 5-6 double-rope rappels down the SE Face; individual station lengths aren't given explicitly. An alternate option reverses the South Ridge itself via numerous short single-rope rappels off slings instead. Per-station distances are not published for this descent and are recorded as unknown rather than estimated from a rope's length.

rappel_detail.notes: First of the SE Face double-rope rappels, down the gully/slab system toward the Taboo Glacier.
Second station positioned climber's left of the fall line.
rappel_detail.station: This is the one station on the sequence that is off the fall line — it sits climber's left. Every other station on the face is either straight below the one above it or climber's right, so left is the exception to look for rather than the rule.

rappel_detail.pull: Double-rope rappel like the rest of the sequence. Send the first person down carrying a picket, axe and crampons so they can climb out of the moat and protect whoever follows; nobody above can help once the ropes are pulled.
rappel_detail.notes: Crux rappel: must cross a moat/bergschrund at the bottom to reach the snowfield below.
hazards: The rappel ends in a moat/bergschrund between the rock and the snowfield rather than on the snow, and its size cannot be judged from the route or from the col on the way in
Parties have had to be lowered into the moat and ice-climb out the far side, or drop into it, traverse a few hundred feet inside, and then cross a steep unstable glacier lip
Reports describe the moat as deep enough that it would have been uncrossable a week later in the season — late-season parties should expect it open
rappel_detail.station: The final station is on your left as you come down toward the last cliff above the snow. Find it before you commit over that edge — it is not on the lip you are walking toward.

current.descent_text: Three options exist, and the choice depends on party speed and whether you're continuing to Forbidden Peak. (1) Reverse the South Ridge: downclimb interspersed with numerous short, traversing rappels off fixed slings/anchors that are 'in abundance' along the ridge — a single rope is generally sufficient for these short raps, but carry extra webbing/cord to back up or replace tat, since stations are alpine-style (slung horns, chockstones, occasional old fixed gear) rather than bolted. This option is slower but avoids the moat problems of the SE Face line. (2) Descend the Southeast Face: downclimb from the summit area to the top rappel station, then make 5-6 double-rope (60m) rappels down the SE Face gully/slab system back toward the Taboo Glacier — the second station is on climber's left, the rest are straight down or climber's right. The crux of this option is the final rappel, where you must cross a moat/bergschrund to reach the snowfield below; this can be genuinely difficult and its condition can't be scoped from above, so the first person down should carry a picket, ice axe, and crampons to help climb out of the moat if needed. Bring two ropes (or a single rope doubled) for these double-rope rappels. (3) Continue over the summit and descend via the Torment-Forbidden Traverse toward Forbidden Peak (sustained exposure, a 5.6 step and ~45-degree snow/ice) if that's the day's objective — this is a full traverse, not a simple descent, and commits you to exiting via Forbidden's West Ridge/Boston Basin instead of returning the way you came.
